data.targetWord: The Christian belief that God became human in the person of Jesus Christ — the theological meaning behind Christmas

examples.en-GB: Christmas celebrates the incarnation — the moment God entered human history as a baby.

data.targetWord: The four-week period of preparation and waiting before Christmas in the Christian calendar, beginning on the fourth Sunday before 25 December

examples.en-GB: Many Christians use an Advent calendar to count down the days to Christmas.

data.targetWord: The most important Christian festival, celebrating the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead — the foundation of Christian hope

examples.en-GB: Easter Sunday marks the resurrection and is the central celebration of the Christian year.

data.targetWord: A 40-day period of fasting, prayer, and reflection before Easter, representing Jesus's 40 days of temptation in the wilderness

examples.en-GB: Many Christians give up something for Lent as a form of self-discipline and spiritual focus.

data.targetWord: The Christian belief that Jesus rose from the dead three days after his crucifixion — the event celebrated at Easter

examples.en-GB: The resurrection is the foundation of Christian faith and the meaning behind Easter Sunday.

data.targetWord: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar — a month of fasting from dawn to sunset, increased prayer, and Qur'an recitation (not technically a festival)

examples.en-GB: During Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn to sunset and focus on prayer and reflection.

data.targetWord: The Festival of Breaking the Fast — a celebration marking the end of Ramadan, featuring communal prayers, feasting, and gift-giving

examples.en-GB: Eid al-Fitr begins with a special communal prayer and is a time for families to celebrate together.

data.targetWord: The Festival of Sacrifice — commemorating Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God, celebrated with prayer and the sharing of meat with those in need

examples.en-GB: Eid al-Adha remembers Ibrahim's act of obedience and the importance of submission to God.

data.targetWord: Passover — the Jewish festival commemorating the Exodus from Egypt, when God freed the Israelites from slavery under Pharaoh

examples.en-GB: Families gather for the Seder meal on Pesach to retell the story of the Exodus from Egypt.

data.targetWord: The Passover meal — a ritual feast during which the Exodus story is retold using symbolic foods and the reading of the Haggadah

examples.en-GB: At the Seder table, bitter herbs represent the bitterness of slavery and matzah represents the haste of the Exodus.

data.targetWord: The Day of Atonement — the holiest day in the Jewish year, marked by a 25-hour fast, prayer, and seeking forgiveness from God and others

examples.en-GB: Yom Kippur is a solemn day for reflection, confession, and seeking reconciliation with God.

data.targetWord: The Jewish New Year — a two-day festival of prayer, reflection, and the sounding of the shofar (ram's horn), beginning the Ten Days of Repentance

examples.en-GB: The sound of the shofar at Rosh Hashanah calls Jews to repentance and self-examination.

data.targetWord: A musical instrument made from a ram's horn, blown during Rosh Hashanah and at the end of Yom Kippur as a call to repentance and attention

examples.en-GB: The sound of the shofar is a traditional call to wake up spiritually and examine one's actions.

data.targetWord: The Hindu Festival of Lights, celebrating the victory of light over darkness, good over evil, and knowledge over ignorance — associated with Lakshmi and the story of Rama and Sita

examples.en-GB: At Diwali, homes are lit with diyas to welcome Lakshmi and celebrate the return of Rama and Sita.

data.targetWord: The Hindu Festival of Colours — a joyful spring festival celebrating the victory of devotion over evil, associated with the story of Prahlad and Holika

examples.en-GB: Holi is celebrated by throwing coloured powder and water, marking the arrival of spring.

data.targetWord: The most important Sikh festival, marking the founding of the Khalsa (community of committed Sikhs) by Guru Gobind Singh in 1699, celebrated on 13/14 April

examples.en-GB: Vaisakhi is celebrated with processions, kirtan, and the reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

data.targetWord: A Sikh festival or holy day marking the birthday or martyrdom of one of the ten Sikh Gurus, celebrated with Akhand Path (continuous reading of the Guru Granth Sahib)

examples.en-GB: The Gurpurb marking Guru Nanak's birthday is one of the most widely celebrated in the Sikh calendar.

data.targetWord: A continuous, uninterrupted reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib from beginning to end, taking approximately 48 hours, performed at Gurpurbs and other special occasions

examples.en-GB: Volunteers take turns reading during Akhand Path so the recitation continues without break.

data.targetWord: The most important Buddhist festival, celebrated on the May full moon, marking the birth, enlightenment, and death (parinirvana) of the Buddha

examples.en-GB: Vesak is observed with lantern processions, offerings at temples, and meditation.

data.targetWord: The final passing away or death of the Buddha, when he entered complete nirvana — one of the three events commemorated at Vesak

examples.en-GB: Vesak commemorates the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, and parinirvana as a single festival.

data.targetWord: A minor Jewish festival of lights lasting eight days, commemorating the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem — often over-emphasised because it falls near Christmas

examples.en-GB: Hanukkah is a minor festival in the Jewish calendar but is often well known because it falls near Christmas.

data.targetWord: The Islamic practice of fasting — one of the Five Pillars of Islam, observed throughout the month of Ramadan from dawn to sunset

examples.en-GB: Sawm during Ramadan teaches self-discipline, gratitude, and empathy for those who go hungry.

data.targetWord: A Sikh festival meaning 'Day of Liberation', marking the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment — celebrated at the same time as Diwali

examples.en-GB: Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas with fireworks and lights, which coincides with the Hindu festival of Diwali.

data.targetWord: The Christian day commemorating the crucifixion and death of Jesus Christ — part of Holy Week before Easter Sunday

examples.en-GB: Good Friday is a solemn day of reflection on Christ's suffering and death before the joy of Easter.

data.targetWord: A small clay oil lamp lit during Diwali and other Hindu festivals to symbolise the victory of light over darkness

examples.en-GB: Rows of diyas are placed around doorways and windowsills during Diwali to welcome the goddess Lakshmi.

data.title: Put the main events of the Christian year in calendar order, starting with Advent.
items: Advent — four weeks of preparation before Christmas
Christmas (25 December) — celebrating the birth of Jesus
Lent begins — 40 days of fasting and reflection
Good Friday — commemorating the crucifixion of Jesus
Easter Sunday — celebrating the resurrection of Jesus

data.title: Put these Jewish festivals and observances in the correct order of the Jewish calendar year.
items: Rosh Hashanah — Jewish New Year, sounding of the shofar
Yom Kippur — Day of Atonement, 25-hour fast
Hanukkah — eight-day festival of lights (minor festival)
Pesach — Passover, Seder meal retelling the Exodus story
Shavuot — festival celebrating the giving of the Torah

data.title: Put these stages of the Islamic festival cycle in the correct order.
items: The month of Ramadan begins — fasting from dawn to sunset
Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power) — the night the Qur'an was first revealed
The final fast of Ramadan is broken at sunset
Eid al-Fitr — Festival of Breaking the Fast, communal prayers and celebration
Eid al-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice, commemorating Ibrahim's obedience
